newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech government wants concrete bank selloff plan.
newsitem.headline: Czech government wants concrete bank selloff plan.

text.p: The Czech government on Wednesday called on the central bank to submit a "more concrete" plan to privatise shares in the four largest banks, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said.
Last week, the Czech National Bank (CNB) proposed to the cabinet a broad plan to privatise the state's major holdings in the country's "Big Four" banks.

The CNB said its plan came from the point of view of a banking sector regulator aiming to make Czech banks more prepared for foreign competition, especially when the country enters the European Union.
The plan included selling the state's 31.5-percent stake in IPB a.s. to a top foreign investor and merging Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka (CSOB) with savings bank Ceska Sporitelna.
Japan-based investment bank Nomura and Dutch ING Bank have expressed interest in the IPB stake, Czech officials said.

Klaus, who welcomed news of Nomura's possible interest in IPB, said on Wednesday he hoped new CNB details "would go beyond" the suggestions already submitted but did not elaborate on what he expected in the new report, due "in the coming days."

Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik, however, said on Wednesday that "partial" decisions on the privatisation of the Big Four could come at next week's regular cabinet meeting. Those decisions could include concrete decisions on the sale of IPB shares, he said.
Asked whether the decisions would be on principles or on concrete steps of banking privatisation, Kocarnik said "I think it can be both.
"Basically, there is a consensus concerning IPB... so there can be also a decision made that it will be sold off," he told reporters after leaving a cabinet meeting.

Last week, IPB said its top management had "constructive dialogue" with senior Nomura officials about the sale of IPB shares but said further decisions would depend on the government and central bank.
Kocarnik, who backs plans to sell the IPB holding to a strategic foreign partner, said the stake would be sold through a tender, if approved.
Meanwhile, a CSOB and Sporitelna merger would create the largest bank in Eastern Europe with combined assets topping 540 billion Czech crowns ($20.11 billion).
But the prime minister frowned upon plans for a Sporitelna/CSOB merger last weekend when he said it was akin to fusing Prague's two top soccer teams, something unthinkable for Czechs.

The CNB, in its gradual approach proposal last week, said it would prefer to wait on the final privatisation of the new combined Sporitelna and CSOB for three to five years until the effects of the merger are analysed.
Separately, the CNB's plan last week also called for a delay in privatisating the state's remaining roughly 49-percent stake in Komercni Banka a.s., the largest commercial bank.
